The first thing Ada repaired was a toaster that had forgotten what bread was.

It sat on her workbench with an air of injured dignity, rejecting every slice she offered. The heating elements worked. The lever worked. Even the little dial, which promised a spectrum from pale gold to archaeological charcoal, turned smoothly. But the bread sprang back out as if the machine objected on principle.

“Fair enough,” Ada told it. “We all lose track.”

She cleaned its contacts, replaced a tired spring, and discovered a marble wedged beneath the carriage.

After that, it remembered.

***

Her repair shop occupied the narrowest building on Bellwether Street. Between a pharmacy and a bakery, it looked less like a business than a gap someone had reluctantly roofed over. The sign above the window said ADA VALE: REPAIRS, and below that, in smaller letters, MOST THINGS.

People occasionally asked what the exception was.

“Depends on the week,” she said.

She repaired lamps, radios, kitchen chairs, music boxes, and the peculiar mechanical birds that had been fashionable thirty years earlier. Once, she repaired a velvet curtain by introducing its owner to a woman named June.

She considered that a successful repair.

***

One wet Thursday, a boy arrived carrying a cardboard box.

He was perhaps ten, with rain flattened into his hair and the stern expression children wear when they have decided not to cry.

“My grandfather said you fix things.”

“Sometimes.”

The boy placed the box on her counter. Inside lay a pocket watch, a grocery receipt, and a photograph of a man standing beside an enormous pumpkin.

“The watch?” Ada asked.

“The afternoon.”

She waited.

“The last afternoon I saw him. I spent it playing a game on my mother’s phone.”

Outside, a bus exhaled at the curb.

“I want it back.”

***

Ada had learned that impossible requests deserved a chair.

She pulled one over and put the kettle on.

“What’s your name?”

“Eli.”

“And your grandfather?”

“Granddad.”

“A good name.”

He gave her a suspicious look, checking for mockery. Finding none, he sat.

Ada examined the watch. Its case was scratched, its glass intact. The hands pointed to twenty past four.

“When did it stop?”

“I don’t know.”

She wound it gently. Nothing happened.

Eli watched her fingers.

“You can fix it?”

“The watch, probably.”

“And the afternoon?”

The kettle began its small, rising argument with the silence.

“Tell me about it,” she said.

***

At first, Eli remembered only the phone.

There had been a game involving towers and bright, furious creatures. He had nearly reached a difficult level. His grandfather had been talking, and Eli had said “Uh-huh” several times without listening.

“What was he wearing?” Ada asked.

“The brown cardigan.”

“Was it cold?”

“No. He always wore it.”

“What could you smell?”

Eli frowned.

“Tomatoes.”

Ada set two mugs on the counter. His contained mostly milk.

“He was making lunch?”

“No. We were in the greenhouse.”

A little space opened in his expression.

“There was a cracked pane. He’d taped it.”

***

The afternoon returned reluctantly, in pieces too ordinary to have seemed worth keeping.

His grandfather had watered the seedlings with a red jug. A bee had battered itself against the glass, ignoring the open door. Somewhere beyond the garden wall, someone was cutting timber.

“He said the bee was like Uncle Martin,” Eli remembered.

“Why?”

“I don’t know. He laughed.”

“What happened next?”

Eli looked down at the photograph.

“He gave me a tomato.”

“Was it good?”

“It was warm.”

He said this with surprise, as though warmth were information he had just received.

“I dropped some on my shirt.”

***

Ada opened the watch.

Inside, a small brass wheel had come loose. She found the escaped screw caught in a fold of the mechanism and set it carefully in a tray.

Eli leaned forward.

“Is that all?”

“That’s enough.”

While she worked, he remembered his grandfather finding a cloth to wipe the tomato juice. He remembered being irritated by the fuss.

“Was that before the game?” Ada asked.

“During. I had to pause it.”

The boy rubbed a mark on his sleeve.

“He asked if I wanted another one.”

“Did you?”

“Yes.”

Ada fitted the wheel back into place and checked it under her magnifying lamp.

***

“Did you ever do something like that?” Eli asked.

“Pay attention to the wrong thing?”

He nodded.

“My mother called while I was assembling a wardrobe. I let it ring because I was holding the door straight.”

“Did she die?”

“Not that day. Four years later.”

“Oh.”

“I called her back after supper. She wanted to know whether I needed curtains.”

“Did you?”

“Yes. But I said no.”

Eli considered this.

“Why?”

“I wanted to choose them myself.”

“Did you get ugly ones?”

“Terrible ones.”

He smiled into his mug, and Ada tightened the screw.

***

When the watch began ticking, Eli flinched.

The sound was surprisingly loud.

Ada closed the case and passed it across the counter.

“You haven’t fixed the afternoon,” he said.

“No.”

He held the watch against his ear.

“I still wish I’d listened.”

“I know.”

“Maybe he said something important.”

“Maybe. Did he often?”

“Sometimes he just complained about slugs.”

Ada nodded.

“He hated those,” Eli said.

He finished his milk while she wrote out the receipt. She charged him for the screw, although she had used the old one.

He paid with coins from a purse shaped like a football.

***

The following Thursday, Eli returned with his mother’s desk fan.

“It rattles,” he announced.

Ada plugged it in. The fan made a noise like cutlery falling downstairs.

“An accurate diagnosis.”

He watched her remove the guard. Then he took a folded sheet of paper from his pocket.

“I wrote down the greenhouse,” he said. “Mum helped. She knew why he laughed about Uncle Martin.”

He left the paper beside the fan while he went to the bakery.

Ada didn’t unfold it. She moved it clear of the screws, where he would see it when he came back.
